notes.body: Every CI/CD pipeline, regardless of tool, runs the same logical gauntlet. (1) Source: a commit lands on a tracked branch and triggers the pipeline. (2) Build: compile code, resolve dependencies, and run linters — produce binaries or bytecode. (3) Test: execute the automated suite, cheapest tests first. (4) Scan: static analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, and secret detection. (5) Package: build an immutable artifact (container image, zip, Helm chart) and tag it with the commit SHA. (6) Deploy: promote the artifact through environments toward production, with gates between them. Worked example: a developer pushes commit a1b2c3d fixing a null check. The pipeline compiles the Java service (Build, 40s), runs 240 unit tests (Test, 90s), scans with a CVE database (Scan, 60s), builds image orders-api:a1b2c3d (Package, 45s), and deploys to staging (Deploy, 30s). Total feedback time is about four and a half minutes, and every step is reproducible from the SHA. The key discipline: the artifact built once in Package is the same artifact deployed everywhere — you never rebuild between staging and production, because rebuilding reintroduces untested variance.
notes.title: From Commit to Release: The Six Pipeline Phases

notes.body: Ask a panel where pipelines catch the most defects and the honest answer is unit tests, run early and fast. The reasoning is economic: a bug caught by a unit test costs seconds of compute; the same bug caught in production costs incident response, rollback, and customer trust. Unit tests run in milliseconds each, need no infrastructure, and map one-to-one onto the code that just changed, so they give the tightest feedback loop in the pipeline. Worked example: a pull request changes a discount-calculation function. The pipeline runs 1,800 unit tests in 22 seconds; two fail because the new branch mishandles a zero-quantity edge case. The developer fixes it before any container is built, before any scan runs, before any environment is touched. Had the failure surfaced only in the staging integration tests 20 minutes later, the developer would have context-switched twice. Design rule: order your Test phase by cost — unit first, then integration, then end-to-end — and make the cheap phase a hard gate. If unit tests fail, nothing downstream runs; you do not spend scan and packaging minutes on code already known to be broken.
notes.title: Where Pipelines Stop Code Most: Unit Tests

notes.body: A quality gate is a policy checkpoint inside a pipeline: a measurable condition that must hold before the pipeline may proceed. Gates differ from tests in that they assert properties of the whole change, not behaviors of individual functions. Typical gates: unit-test pass rate of 100 percent, line coverage at or above 80 percent, zero critical-severity CVEs in dependencies, no secrets detected in the diff, and lint with zero errors. Worked example: a team sets a coverage gate of 80 percent. A PR adds 200 new lines but only 120 are covered by tests, dragging total coverage from 84 to 77 percent. The gate fails the build at the Test phase, the artifact is never packaged, and the developer gets a precise message: add tests for the uncovered branches in billing.py. Without the gate, the under-tested code would have shipped silently. Implement gates as first-class pipeline steps that exit non-zero on violation, not as advisory warnings humans must remember to read. A gate that only warns is decoration; a gate that blocks is policy. Keep the gate list short and stable — every gate you add taxes every future build, so each one must earn its minutes.
notes.title: Quality Gates: Fail Fast, Fail Cheap

notes.body: Branching strategy decides how often code integrates, and integration frequency decides how painful merges are. Trunk-based development has every developer commit to a single main branch at least daily, behind feature flags when work is incomplete; releases are cut from trunk whenever it is green. GitFlow maintains long-lived develop and master branches plus feature, release, and hotfix branches, with formal merge ceremonies between them. Trunk-based minimizes merge conflicts and keeps the pipeline fast because there is one branch to keep green; it demands strong test coverage and feature flags, since half-finished work lands on main. GitFlow gives explicit control over what goes into each release, which suits scheduled, audited releases, but merge debt accumulates and the pipeline must validate many branch combinations. Worked example: a five-person team shipping a SaaS product weekly chooses trunk-based with flags; their pipeline stays under five minutes and merges are trivial. A bank shipping a core ledger quarterly with regulatory sign-off chooses GitFlow; the release branch gets a dedicated hardening pipeline. Interview line: pick the strategy that matches release cadence and risk tolerance, and be able to defend the trade.
notes.title: Trunk-Based Development vs GitFlow

notes.body: Environments are isolated copies of the system at different trust levels, and promotion is the controlled movement of one immutable artifact upward through them. Dev is the developer's sandbox: fast, disposable, seeded with fake data. QA or staging mirrors production as closely as affordable — same container images, same database engine, realistic data volumes — because this is where integration, performance, and acceptance tests run. Production is the real system with real data and real users, and nothing enters it except through the pipeline. Worked example: image payments:9f2e1a passes unit tests and scans, then deploys to staging where a load test reveals a connection-pool leak. The image is rejected in staging, fixed in a new commit, and only image payments:44bd07c — built once, tested everywhere — is promoted to production. Environment parity is what makes staging results trustworthy: if staging runs a different database version than production, a green staging run proves nothing. Rollback is promotion in reverse — redeploy the previous known-good artifact tag, which is why every artifact carries its commit SHA and every deployment is recorded.
notes.title: Environments: Dev, Stage/QA, Prod and Promotion

notes.body: When a pipeline goes red, the fastest engineers triage by phase, not by panic. First, read which phase failed — Build, Test, Scan, Package, Deploy — because the phase tells you the category of the problem. Second, read the first failing assertion or command, not the last log line; everything after the first failure is usually cascade noise. Third, reproduce the smallest failing unit locally before touching the pipeline. Worked example: a run fails in the Scan phase with 'CRITICAL CVE-2024-XXXX in libfoo 2.3'. The first failure is the scanner exit code, not the 400 lines of download logs above it. The fix is to bump libfoo to the patched 2.4 in requirements, which you verify locally with the same scanner invocation the pipeline uses, then push. Notice what you did not do: you did not rerun the whole pipeline hoping it passes, and you did not edit the pipeline YAML to skip the scan. Common failure fingerprints to memorize: Build red means dependency or compile error; Test red means behavior regression; Scan red means known vulnerability or leaked secret; Deploy red means environment or configuration drift. State the phase, the first failure, and the smallest reproduction — that is the whole triage method.
notes.title: Anatomy of a Pipeline Failure: Reading the Run

notes.body: Jenkins offers two pipeline dialects. Declarative pipeline is the opinionated, structured form: a pipeline block containing agent, stages, and post sections with a fixed grammar that Jenkins validates before running. Scripted pipeline is raw Groovy on top of the Jenkins DSL — a node block with full programmatic freedom: loops, try/catch, dynamic stage generation. Prefer declarative for nearly everything: it is readable, it fails fast on syntax errors, and Blue Ocean renders it cleanly. Reach for scripted (or a script block inside declarative) only when you need genuine programming — generating stages from a matrix in code, or complex retry logic the declarative directives cannot express. Worked example: a declarative pipeline with stages Checkout, Build, Test, and a post block that always publishes JUnit results covers 90 percent of services. The moment you need 'run the deploy stage once per region in a list fetched from an API at runtime,' you drop a script block inside the declarative stage and write the loop in Groovy. Rule of thumb for the panel: declarative by default, scripted by exception, and be able to name the exception.
notes.title: Declarative vs Scripted Pipelines

notes.body: When a panel asks whether you can write Groovy directly in a Jenkinsfile, they are checking that you know a Jenkinsfile IS a Groovy script executed by the Jenkins pipeline engine — not a YAML file with steps. That means Groovy semantics apply: single-quoted strings are plain, double-quoted strings interpolate ${variables}, def declares local variables, and closures like { ... } appear in post conditions and parallel branches. Worked example: in environment { IMAGE = "orders-api:${env.BUILD_NUMBER}" }, the double quotes interpolate the build number at runtime, while sh 'echo $IMAGE' uses single quotes so Groovy leaves the dollar sign alone and the shell expands it. A classic bug is sh "docker build -t $IMAGE ." where Groovy interpolates $IMAGE before the shell sees it — correct here, but the same pattern with a password leaks it into the command string. Trace the evaluation order yourself: Groovy first (double quotes only), then the shell. If you can explain which layer expands which variable, you can answer every Groovy-in-Jenkinsfile question the panel has.
notes.title: Groovy in a Jenkinsfile: What the Panel Means

notes.body: The panel question 'how do you standardize Jenkinsfiles across repos' has one canonical answer: Jenkins shared libraries. Without one, forty repositories each carry a copy-pasted Jenkinsfile that drifts — one team pins an old scanner, another forgets the artifact push. A shared library is a separate Git repository Jenkins trusts, with two layouts: vars/ holds global steps as <name>.groovy files exposing a call() method (so vars/standardBuild.groovy is invoked as standardBuild(...)), and src/ holds plain Groovy classes for logic. Worked example — before: every repo's Jenkinsfile repeats 60 lines of checkout, build, test, scan. After: the library provides vars/standardPipeline.groovy with def call(Map config), and each repo's Jenkinsfile shrinks to @Library('corp-pipeline-lib') _ followed by standardPipeline(appName: 'orders-api', testCmd: 'pytest'). One fix to the scan step in the library updates all forty repos on their next build. Version the library with tags (@Library('corp-pipeline-lib@1.4')) so a library change cannot silently break every build at once.
notes.title: Standardizing Jenkinsfiles with Shared Libraries

notes.body: Jenkins must hand secrets to builds — registry passwords, cloud tokens, Terraform API keys — without ever printing them. Credentials binding does exactly that: secrets live in the Jenkins credential store (or an external vault), and the pipeline references them by ID; Jenkins injects them as environment variables and masks them in console output. Two patterns: the environment directive TF_TOKEN = credentials('terraform-cloud-token') binds a secret-text credential for the whole pipeline, and the withCredentials step scopes username/password or secret files to a block. Worked example: withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'acr-creds', usernameVariable: 'REG', passwordVariable: 'REG_PASS')]) { sh 'echo $REG_PASS | docker login myregistry.azurecr.io -u $REG --password-stdin' }. Note the single quotes around the shell command so Groovy never interpolates the secret, and --password-stdin so the password never appears in a process list. This is the same mechanism teams use for Jenkins credential injection of Terraform secrets: the token is bound at runtime, terraform apply reads it from the environment, and the value never lands in the repo, the Jenkinsfile, or the logs.
notes.title: Credentials Binding: Secrets Without Leaks

notes.body: An agent is where pipeline steps execute; a label routes work to the right machine. agent any runs on any available executor, agent { label 'linux-build' } pins the build to nodes carrying that label, and agent { docker { image 'maven:3.9' } } runs the stage inside a container on a capable node. Labels encode capabilities: operating system, installed toolchains, network access to a private registry, or a GPU. Worked example: a monorepo builds a Java service and a Python worker. The Jenkinsfile uses agent { label 'java-17' } for the service stage and agent { label 'python-311' } for the worker stage, so each runs where its toolchain exists instead of installing everything everywhere. A common failure is a pipeline stuck with 'Waiting for next available executor on linux-build' — the triage is to check the Nodes page for offline agents or a label typo, not to rerun the build. Keep labels coarse (linux-build, windows-test, docker-capable) rather than per-project; fine-grained labels fragment the executor pool and builds queue behind idle capacity.
notes.title: Agents, Labels and Executors

notes.body: The post section of a declarative pipeline defines what happens after stages complete, conditioned on the outcome: always, success, failure, unstable, changed. This is where pipelines earn their operational keep — publishing test reports, archiving artifacts, and notifying humans. Worked example: post { always { junit '**/target/surefire-reports/*.xml' } success { archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'dist/*.whl', fingerprint: true } failure { mail to: 'team@example.com', subject: "Build ${env.JOB_NAME} #${env.BUILD_NUMBER} failed" } }. The junit step turns XML into trend graphs; archiveArtifacts with fingerprinting lets Jenkins trace which build produced which artifact; the mail step fires only on failure so the team is not spammed by green builds. Failure hygiene rules: notify the channel that owns the breakage (not the whole company), include the direct link to the failed build (env.BUILD_URL), and keep the console log free of secrets so the failure link is safe to share. A pipeline that publishes results, archives artifacts, and pages the right people on red is a complete pipeline; one that only runs steps is a script.
notes.title: post Blocks, Notifications and Failure Hygiene

notes.body: A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that maps events to automation. The mental model has four layers. Events (on:) decide when the workflow runs: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch for manual runs. Jobs are units of work that run in parallel by default on runners — needs: creates ordering between jobs. Steps inside a job run sequentially on the same runner, each step either a shell run: command or a uses: reference to an action. Runners are the machines: GitHub-hosted (ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest) or self-hosted on your infrastructure. Worked example: on: pull_request targeting main triggers a job test on ubuntu-latest whose steps check out the PR code (actions/checkout@v4), set up Python (actions/setup-python@v5), install requirements, and run pytest. Push a commit to the PR and the workflow reruns automatically — that is CI without a separate server. Secrets live in the repo or organization settings and are referenced as ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}, never hardcoded; the ${{ }} expression syntax is evaluated by Actions before the runner sees the step.
notes.title: GitHub Actions: Events, Jobs, Steps, Runners

notes.body: A matrix strategy runs the same job once per combination of variables you declare, turning one workflow definition into N parallel runs. This is how projects test against multiple Python versions, operating systems, or dependency sets without duplicating YAML. Worked example: strategy: { matrix: { python-version: ['3.11', '3.12'], os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest] } } produces four job instances — 3.11/ubuntu, 3.12/ubuntu, 3.11/windows, 3.12/windows — each running the identical steps with ${{ matrix.python-version }} and ${{ matrix.os }} substituted. Add fail-fast: false when you want every combination to report even if one fails, so a Windows-only failure does not hide behind an early abort. Cost awareness matters: a 4-way matrix quadruples runner minutes, so matrix over versions you actually support, not every version ever released. The panel loves matrix questions because they test whether you think in terms of configuration space rather than copy-pasted jobs — if your answer to 'test on three OSes' is three jobs, you have missed the feature.
notes.title: Matrix Builds: One Workflow, Many Configurations

notes.body: Jobs run on fresh runners, so anything a later job needs must be persisted explicitly. Artifacts (actions/upload-artifact@v4 and actions/download-artifact@v4) carry files between jobs or preserve them after the run — test reports, built wheels, coverage HTML. Caching (actions/cache@v4) is different: it stores reusable dependencies keyed by a hash of the lock file, so pip or npm installs skip the network on repeat runs. Worked example: job build installs dependencies and uploads dist/ as artifact api-wheel; job test declares needs: build, downloads api-wheel, and runs pytest against it — the wheel travels through Actions storage, not through git. In the same workflow, actions/cache@v4 keyed on hashFiles('requirements.txt') makes the second run's pip install take seconds instead of minutes. Rules: artifacts expire (set retention-days deliberately), never put secrets in artifacts (anyone with repo read access can download them), and cache keys must include the lock-file hash or you will serve stale dependencies. Artifacts move work forward; caches make repeats cheap.
notes.title: Artifacts and Caching: Passing Work Between Jobs

notes.body: When ten repositories need the same CI, copy-pasting workflow YAML recreates the Jenkinsfile-drift problem from module 38. Reusable workflows solve it: a workflow with on: workflow_call declares typed inputs and secrets, and caller workflows invoke it with uses:. Worked example: the platform team publishes .github/workflows/python-ci.yml in a central repo with on: { workflow_call: { inputs: { python-version: { required: true, type: string } }, secrets: { pypi-token: { required: true } } } }. Each service repo then has a four-line workflow: on: push; jobs: { ci: { uses: org/platform/.github/workflows/python-ci.yml@main, with: { python-version: '3.12' }, secrets: { pypi-token: ${{ secrets.PYPI_TOKEN }} } } }. One fix to the central workflow updates every caller on their next run; pinning @main vs @v1.2 is the same versioning trade as Jenkins library tags. Note the constraints: the called workflow's jobs cannot directly use the caller's secrets unless declared and passed, and reusable workflows must live in the same or a referenced repository — they are composition, not inheritance.
notes.title: Reusable Workflows: DRY for Pipelines

notes.body: Azure DevOps expresses pipelines in azure-pipelines.yml with a four-level hierarchy: stages contain jobs, jobs contain steps, and steps run tasks or scripts. A stage typically maps to an environment (Build, Deploy-Dev, Deploy-Prod) with approvals between them; jobs within a stage can target different pools. Templates are the reuse mechanism: - template: templates/build.yml with parameters: factors out common steps the way shared libraries do in Jenkins. Worked example: trigger: [main] on pool vmImage ubuntu-latest, a Build stage with a job that uses the UsePythonVersion@0 task, runs pip install and pytest as script steps, then publishes results with PublishTestResults@2. A second Deploy stage dependsOn: Build and carries a deployment job targeting an environment with a manual approval check. Variables and variable groups hold configuration; secret variables are masked in logs like Jenkins credentials. For the panel: Azure DevOps shines where the team already lives in Azure — service connections to subscriptions, boards-to-pipelines traceability, and environments with approval gates map naturally onto enterprise release processes.
notes.title: Azure DevOps Pipelines: Stages, Jobs, Templates

notes.body: All three platforms run the same six pipeline phases from module 37; they differ in hosting, expression, and ecosystem fit. Jenkins is self-hosted and Groovy-based: maximum control, any agent you can provision, but you own upgrades, security, and scaling the controller. GitHub Actions is SaaS and YAML-based, colocated with the code: zero infrastructure, a vast marketplace of actions, per-minute billing — ideal when the repo already lives on GitHub. Azure DevOps is SaaS and YAML-based with first-class enterprise constructs: environments with approvals, service connections, variable groups, and tight Azure integration — ideal for Microsoft-centric enterprises. Worked example decision: a startup with all code on GitHub and no ops team picks Actions (no servers, marketplace actions cover everything). A bank standardized on Azure with change-advisory approvals picks Azure DevOps (environments plus approvals match the governance model). A team needing builds on exotic on-prem hardware picks Jenkins with custom agents. Panel line: there is no best platform, only best fit — name the team's constraints (hosting, governance, ecosystem) and match them.
notes.title: Choosing a Platform: Jenkins vs Actions vs Azure DevOps

handsOnLab.brief: Using the Azure CLI against your own subscription, you will build the Terraform scenario's target by hand: a storage account with per-container access types, a Key Vault holding a secret, diagnostic routing to Log Analytics, and a policy guardrail — then verify everything with read-only commands.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: az storage container show reports off/blob/container respectively; the secret round-trips; the Activity log lists the creation events; the policy assignment appears at the resource-group scope.
handsOnLab.deliverable: A resource group containing a StorageV2 account with three correctly-typed containers, a Key Vault with a retrievable secret and AuditEvent diagnostics flowing, and an Allowed-locations policy assignment — plus a lab-notes file with the resource IDs.
steps: Sign in with az login and set your subscription: az account set --subscription '<your-subscription-id-or-name>'.
Create the resource group: az group create --name rg-il28-lab --location eastus.

Create the storage account: az storage account create --name st<your-initials>il2801 --resource-group rg-il28-lab --location eastus --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2 (keep the name 3–24 chars, lowercase alnum).
Create three containers with different access types: raw-uploads (--public-access off), thumbnails (--public-access blob), public-assets (--public-access container).
Upload a sample file to raw-uploads with az storage blob upload, then verify each container's access type with az storage container show.
Create the Key Vault: az keyvault create --name kv-<your-initials>-il28 --resource-group rg-il28-lab --location eastus.
Store a secret: az keyvault secret set --vault-name <vault> --name db-password --value 'LabOnly-1234!'; retrieve it with az keyvault secret show and confirm the value round-trips.
Create a Log Analytics workspace: az monitor log-analytics workspace create --resource-group rg-il28-lab --workspace-name law-il28-lab.

Enable diagnostics on the vault: az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name kv-diag --resource <vault-resource-id> --workspace <workspace-resource-id> --logs '[{"category":"AuditEvent","enabled":true}]' (get IDs with az keyvault show / az monitor log-analytics workspace show --query id).
Query the control plane: az monitor activity-log list --resource-group rg-il28-lab --max-events 5 -o table; identify your storage account creation event.

Find the built-in policy ID: az policy definition list --query "[?displayName=='Allowed locations'].id" -o tsv; then assign it to the resource group limited to eastus with az policy assignment create --name allowed-locations-il28 --policy <id> --params '{"listOfAllowedLocations":{"value":["eastus"]}}' --scope <rg-id>.

Verify: az policy assignment list --scope <rg-id> -o table shows the assignment; az vm list-usage --location eastus -o table shows current vCPU quota headroom. Document all four resource IDs in a lab-notes file.
handsOnLab.title: Provision Azure Core: Storage, Key Vault, Diagnostics, and Policy

mockTask.q: Panel: 'The dev team needs a storage account. They gave you three container names, and now the requirements changed — each container needs a different access type: private, blob, and container. How do you codify this in Terraform?'

notes.body: An Azure storage account is the container for all Azure Storage data services — blobs, files, queues, tables — and it is exactly what the dev team's Terraform scenario provisions. Three decisions define one: the name, which must be 3–24 characters, lowercase letters and numbers only, globally unique (stdataeast001 is valid; ST_Data-East is not); the performance/redundancy choice — Standard vs Premium tier, and LRS (three copies in one datacenter), ZRS (across zones), GRS (paired region); and the kind, usually StorageV2 (general-purpose v2) which supports all services and tiers. Worked example: the dev team needs durable object storage for nightly exports in East US. You choose name stexportseastus01, Standard tier, GRS for region-pair durability, kind StorageV2. In Terraform that is azurerm_storage_account with account_tier = "Standard", account_replication_type = "GRS". The panel checks two things here: that you know the naming constraints (they break many first attempts) and that you can justify the redundancy choice against cost — GRS doubles the storage bill versus LRS, so you pick it only when regional outage survival is a real requirement.
notes.title: Storage Accounts: The Terraform Scenario's Target

notes.body: Inside a storage account, blob containers hold the objects, and each container carries an access type that is a security decision: private (called off in the CLI) means every request needs authorization; blob means anonymous read access to individual blobs but not listing; container means anonymous read plus anonymous listing of the container's contents. The Terraform scenario's twist — requirements changing to per-container access types — is exactly why the module 34 solution iterates over a map of name → access type instead of a list of names. Worked example: the team asks for three containers: raw-uploads (private — unprocessed customer data), thumbnails (blob — the web app fetches images by direct URL), public-assets (container — a static site lists and serves files). In Terraform: variable "containers" = { raw-uploads = "private", thumbnails = "blob", public-assets = "container" } with for_each over the map and container_access_type = each.value. Interview rule: default everything to private and justify each relaxation. An anonymous-listable container holding anything sensitive is a breach waiting for a scanner to find.
notes.title: Blob Containers and Access Types: private, blob, container

notes.body: Azure Key Vault is the managed store for secrets (passwords, tokens, connection strings), cryptographic keys, and certificates — the place application credentials live instead of app settings or repos. The security model has two layers: the vault's firewall and access control decide who can reach the vault, and access policies (or Azure RBAC) decide which identities may get, list, or set which secrets. Worked example: the payments API needs a database password. You create the vault (az keyvault create --name kv-payments-east --resource-group rg-payments), store the secret (az keyvault secret set --vault-name kv-payments-east --name db-password --value '...'), grant the app's managed identity the 'Key Vault Secrets User' role, and the app fetches the password at startup via the vault URI — the value never appears in configuration files or pipeline logs. Rotation hygiene: enable rotation where the service supports it, version secrets (each set creates a new version), and alert on near-expiry for certificates. The panel's Key Vault questions always circle back to the same principle: no secret in code, no secret in config, no secret in logs — the vault is the single source of truth and managed identity is how workloads prove who they are.
notes.title: Key Vault: Secrets, Keys, Certificates

notes.body: Azure Monitor collects two fundamentally different signal types. Metrics are numeric time series (CPU percent, request count, blob capacity) — cheap, near-real-time, retained briefly, and the basis for alerts. Logs are rich records (who did what, full request details) — verbose, queryable with KQL in a Log Analytics workspace, retained longer, and the basis for investigation. Diagnostic settings are the bridge: you enable them per resource to route its platform logs and metrics to a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an event hub. Worked example: to audit Key Vault access, you create a workspace (az monitor log-analytics workspace create), then az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name kv-diag --resource <vault-id> --workspace <workspace-id> --logs '[{"category":"AuditEvent","enabled":true}]'. Then in the workspace you run KQL: AzureDiagnostics | where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.KEYVAULT" | where OperationName == "SecretGet" | project TimeGenerated, CallerIPAddress, ResultType. Metrics would tell you secret-gets per minute spiked; only the logs tell you which IP did it. Panel line: metrics for alerting, logs for investigating, diagnostic settings to connect the resource to the workspace.
notes.title: Azure Monitor: Metrics, Logs, Diagnostics

notes.body: Azure Policy is governance as code: definitions express rules ('resources must be in East US', 'only approved VM SKUs'), assignments scope them to a management group, subscription, or resource group, and effects decide the behavior — deny blocks the deployment, audit flags it, append/modify remediate it. Worked example: the platform team assigns the built-in 'Allowed locations' policy to the subscription with parameter listOfAllowedLocations = ["eastus"]. A developer's terraform apply targeting West US fails at plan time with a policy denial — the guardrail caught it before any resource existed. Quotas are the other ceiling: each subscription gets limited vCPUs per VM family per region, checked with az vm list-usage --location eastus. Hitting 'quota exceeded' on an AKS scale-up is not a bug; the fix is a support request to raise the quota, not a code change. Two more tools complete the observability picture: Resource Health reports whether Azure itself knows a resource is unhealthy (distinguishing 'my config is broken' from 'the platform is broken'), and Activity logs record every control-plane operation — who created, scaled, or deleted what and when — queryable with az monitor activity-log list.
notes.title: Azure Policy, Quotas and Limits

notes.body: When new AKS nodes fail to appear after scaling, work this checklist in order — it is the panel's expected answer verbatim. (1) Confirm the scale request: az aks nodepool scale --resource-group <rg> --cluster-name <cluster> --name <pool> --node-count <n>, then check the Activity log for the operation's status and error. (2) Cluster autoscaler: if enabled, check its profile and logs — it only scales on unschedulable pods, so no pending pods means no scale. (3) Pending workload: kubectl get events and describe the pending pods; 'Insufficient cpu/memory' tells you the demand side. (4) Quotas: az vm list-usage --location <region> — vCPU quota exhaustion is the most common silent blocker. (5) Region capacity and VM SKU restrictions: the requested SKU may be constrained in that region. (6) Subnet IP space: each node consumes IPs; an exhausted subnet stops scale with no obvious error. (7) Taints, labels, and max pods per node: misconfigured scheduling constraints leave nodes idle. (8) Service principal / managed identity permissions on the VNet and subnet. (9) Azure Policy: a deny assignment (wrong location, disallowed SKU) blocks node creation. (10) Resource Health and Azure Monitor for platform-side issues. Worked example: scale to 5 nodes, only 3 appear. Activity log shows the scale operation succeeded; quotas show 8 of 10 vCPUs used and each node needs 4 — the fourth node cannot fit. The fix is a quota increase, and the evidence trail is quota → Activity log, not guesses.
notes.title: Reference: AKS Node-Troubleshooting Checklist

notes.body: Exposing PaaS services to the internet by default is the opposite of the private-container rule from the storage note. Private Link gives Azure PaaS services — Storage, SQL Database, Key Vault, App Service, Container Registry — a private IP inside your VNet, so traffic never traverses the public internet. The DNS side is where implementations break: you create a Private DNS zone (e.g., privatelink.blob.core.windows.net for storage), link it to the VNet, and the zone carries the A record mapping the service's name to its private IP. Worked example: an AKS cluster must reach a storage account privately. You create the private endpoint in the cluster's VNet, the Private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net with a VNet link, and verify from a pod that stdataeast001.blob.core.windows.net resolves to a 10.x address. For on-premises clients, conditional forwarding sends privatelink.* queries to the Azure DNS resolver. Related panel question: Application Gateway vs Load Balancer — the gateway is Layer 7 (HTTP routing, TLS termination, WAF; the classic browser → DNS → App Gateway → AKS backend-pool flow), while Load Balancer is Layer 4 (TCP/UDP distribution). Choose the gateway when you route by URL or host; choose the load balancer for raw throughput.
